issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these items are hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. 'Story Feels Unreal' and especially 'Overwhelm on Recall' imply a disjointed, emotionally intense trauma memory, which fits the strong Memory↔Threat links. In contrast, 'Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily' suggests unusually easy narrative access to the trauma and directly pulls against the other memory items. For a severe PTSD profile centered on intrusive, overwhelming childhood domestic violence memories, this Memory combination is clinically inconsistent.

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, these two items directly contradict each other: being able to talk about the trauma very easily is incompatible with simultaneously being unable to put the event into words. This is a clear within-node inconsistency.

vignette:
Layla describes her life as being lived behind a pane of glass. At thirty, she feels a profound separation between herself and the world, a constant, low-humming vigilance that has become her baseline. The origins of this feeling are buried in memories she cannot articulate, fragments from a childhood home that was not a sanctuary. She has no coherent story to tell of those years, only a collection of sensory snapshots: the sudden pivot of her father's shoulders in the kitchen, the sharp crack of a hand against skin that was not her own, the thud of her mother's body against the floral wallpaper in their open-plan living room. When she tries to grasp these moments, to line them up into a narrative, a crushing weight descends. It's a purely emotional overwhelm, a wordless dread that forces her to stop, leaving her with the frustrating certainty that she knows what happened but is utterly unable to find the words to describe it.

This inability to rely on her own mind has metastasized into a pervasive self-doubt. She has come to believe that she simply cannot trust herself to do the right thing in a moment of crisis, a belief forged in the paralysis of watching those childhood events unfold, a small girl frozen in a doorway. This conviction shadows every decision. It also fuels a deep and abiding mistrust of others; if the people meant to protect you are the source of the danger, then who is left to trust? This belief system ultimately unraveled her marriage. Her ex-husband, she recalls, could never understand why she couldn't just relax, why a sudden move to embrace her would make her flinch, or why she needed to check the deadbolt on their apartment door three times before bed. He saw it as a rejection of him, when for Layla, it was a fundamental law of survival.

Her work as a bartender has become a nightly exercise in endurance. The bar is a wide, open space, precisely the kind of environment that makes every nerve ending feel exposed and vulnerable. She feels safest behind the physical barrier of the counter, but the job demands constant interaction in the open. Every sudden gesture from a customer-a hand raised to get her attention, an arm slung around a friend's shoulder-sends a jolt of adrenaline through her. She has become an expert at controlling her emotions, keeping her expression placid while her heart hammers against her ribs. Before each shift, she mentally rehearses worst-case scenarios: an aggressive drunk, a fight breaking out, someone following her home. She tells herself this is preparation, but it leaves her perpetually braced for an impact that never comes, arriving at work already exhausted.

The only place the vigilance recedes, even slightly, is her small apartment. This is her one true safe zone. But safety is a project, not a given. The moment she gets home, she engages in a ritual of locking the door, checking the latch, then checking it again. She does the same with her single window, pulling the blinds tight against the outside world. This is the only way to quiet the sense of imminent threat enough to sleep. Over the years, her world has shrunk to the path between this fortified apartment and the bar where she performs a precarious version of normalcy. The consequences have been stark; friendships have faded, invitations have been declined, and her life has become a closed loop of work and solitude. She finally sought therapy after her manager took her aside last week. A customer had dropped a glass, and Layla had physically recoiled so violently that she'd knocked over a tray of drinks. "You seem like you're waiting for the sky to fall, Layla," he'd said, not unkindly. It was the moment she realized the pane of glass was no longer invisible to others. She is terrified of what therapy might uncover, but the exhaustion of holding the sky up all by herself has finally become too much to bear.
